prompt.context: Back in the 1990s, Bain Capital bought Domino's Pizza, a nationwide pizza delivery chain. They wanted to identify a growth strategy. There are four national players in the pizza industry: Pizza Hut (market leader, mainly sit-down stores with some delivery), Domino's (no sit-down, no carry-out, entirely delivery-based, 80% franchisee-owned and 20% company-owned), Little Caesar's (cafeteria-style carry-out only, markets 2 pies for the price of 1, no delivery), and Papa John's (new fast-growing player, carry-out only from high foot-traffic street locations, tagline 'better ingredients, better pizza'). A blind taste test found little preference among the four pizzas, but when brand names were revealed, people preferred Papa John's.
prompt.question: Bain Capital has hired you to identify a growth strategy for Domino's Pizza. How would you approach this, and what would you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost per pizza for a franchisee?
What is the royalty/fee structure that franchisees pay to Domino's corporate?
clarifying_info.a: Franchisees pay 5% of their sales (revenues) to Domino's corporate.

clarifying_info.q: How long are the franchisee contracts?
clarifying_info.a: Contracts are 5 years; Luigi's store is in year 1 of his contract.

framework: Industry landscape: understand competitive positioning of Domino's vs. Pizza Hut, Papa John's, Little Caesar's — business model, strengths, weaknesses
Growth opportunities: identify levers to grow revenue — open new stores, grow same-store sales (volume vs. price), expand product offerings
Store expansion criteria: demographics, cost structure, competitor presence, existing best practices, population growth, pizza demand
Franchisee economics: pricing, unit economics, royalty structure, and alignment between franchisee and corporate incentives
Price strategy: assess impact of price changes on franchisee profit vs. corporate royalty revenue
Franchise governance: mechanisms to control pricing and protect brand across 80% franchisee network

questions.prompt: What are the key factors you would look at to identify where to open new stores?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm a structured list covering: (1) Best practices — where existing high-performing stores are located and what those areas have in common; (2) Competitor landscape — areas with low competitor concentration to capture first-mover advantage; (3) Cost structure — regions with affordable labor and rent; (4) Demographics — pizza skews toward age 13-35, young families; (5) Income — low to middle income areas (high income tends to prefer upscale dining); (6) Population growth — growing or at least stable populations; (7) Geographic gaps — regions where Domino's has no presence; (8) Pizza demand growth — areas where demand for pizza is increasing. Strong candidates note that ideally all factors align.

questions.prompt: What kind of specific location would be a good candidate for a new store?
questions.guidance: University neighborhoods fit best: young demographic (13-35), low income, students order delivery to dorms (aligns with Domino's delivery-only model), enrollment typically grows year over year. Other acceptable answers: suburban strip malls, office park vicinities, near suburban schools, near sporting facilities. Interviewer should ask for reasoning behind each suggestion.

questions.prompt: Luigi, a franchisee, currently sells 100 pizzas per day at $10 each. If he raises the price to $11, he expects to sell 90 pizzas per day. His variable cost is $6 per pizza. Should Luigi raise prices?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for cost data before calculating. Bonus credit for noting fixed costs are irrelevant in the short run (they are the same in both scenarios). Candidate should compute margin and daily profit under both scenarios and compare.

math.setup: Compare daily profit at $10 vs. $11 price point. Variable cost = $6/pizza. Fixed costs cancel out.
math.answer: Luigi should raise the price to $11. He earns $50 more per day.

questions.prompt: Would the price increase benefit Domino's corporate overall?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask about the royalty structure (5% of revenues). Calculate Domino's royalty under both scenarios and compare. Key insight: corporate earns based on revenue (not profit), so the lower revenue at $11 (due to fewer pizzas sold) hurts corporate even though it helps Luigi. Candidate should conclude Domino's corporate should not encourage or allow this price increase, and should have control over franchisee pricing.

math.setup: Domino's receives 5% of franchisee revenue. Compare corporate royalty at $10 vs. $11.
math.answer: Domino's corporate revenue decreases by $0.50/day per store. If Luigi's price elasticity is typical across the chain, Domino's should not raise prices — it benefits the franchisee but hurts corporate royalty income.

questions.prompt: What can Domino's do to control prices at the store level — first with Luigi specifically, then at the national level?
questions.guidance: For Luigi: remind him the $50 short-run gain is likely temporary — long-run, inelastic demand will erode as customers switch to competitors. The blind taste test result (people see all pizzas as comparable except Papa John's) supports this argument. For national level: franchisee contracts should designate Domino's corporate as the price setter, or require corporate approval for any price changes. Additional lever: Domino's controls national marketing and advertising — embedding the $10 price in ads effectively forces franchisees to honor it (customers will complain if the advertised price differs from in-store price).

brainstorming.prompt: What factors would you look at to identify where to open new Domino's stores?

categories.name: Competitive landscape
ideas: Areas with low concentration of pizza competitors
Regions where Domino's is first mover
Avoid markets saturated with Pizza Hut, Papa John's, or Little Caesar's

categories.name: Demographics
ideas: Areas near schools or sporting facilities

categories.name: Socioeconomic
ideas: Avoid high-income neighborhoods that prefer upscale restaurants

categories.name: Geographic gaps
ideas: Regions with no existing Domino's presence

categories.name: Demand signals
ideas: Growing demand for pizza in the area

recommendation: Open more stores in high-potential areas that match Domino's delivery model: university towns, suburban areas with young families, office parks, and regions with low competitor presence
Do not raise prices — while a price increase boosts individual franchisee profit, it reduces total corporate royalty revenue because the fee is based on revenue, not profit

Establish and enforce pricing governance: ensure all franchisee contracts give Domino's corporate price-setting authority or require prior approval for price changes; use national advertising at fixed price points to reinforce compliance
risks: Franchisees may resist pricing controls, especially those mid-contract
Papa John's growing brand preference (blind taste test) could limit Domino's ability to grow same-store sales without brand investment
Expanding into new markets requires capital and operational bandwidth that may strain quality control
next_steps: Audit existing high-performing stores to define the ideal location profile
Map geographic white-spaces with favorable demographic and competitive characteristics
Review and revise standard franchisee contract terms to include price-setting authority
Develop brand and marketing investment plan to address Papa John's brand perception gap
